records.comment_text: 5. The methodology also mentions some very specific methodologic terminology (Greenhouse-Geisser correction, Bonferroni correction, violation of normality assumption requirement) which not all readers may be familiar with and may need a little more context.
records.response_text:
Response: Thank you for the comment. I agree with the reviewer that clarification would help readers not familiar with statistical analysis. Hence, I have added the following brief explanation in the methodological section as follows:
“In a split-plot design, sphericity, or the assumption that the variances of differences between all combinations of related conditions are equal, might be violated and caused inflated or deflated Type I error in the results from F-tests. Hence, Greenhouse-Geisser correction was applied to data when the assumption of sphericity was violated. Furthermore, due to the repeated measurement involved in the split-plot design, Bonferroni correction was utilized to control the probability of a Type I error from multiple hypothesis tests between different time points.”

records.comment_text: 1. The authors have yet to effectively demonstrate to the reviewers the rationale behind their exclusive use of TEM-4's writing prompts, instead of incorporating the TEM-4 scoring rubric. Furthermore, it is essential for them to clarify why they have chosen to utilize scoring rubrics from other scholars, particularly when these rubrics are claimed to align with the specific research goals presented in the article. Providing this justification is crucial for strengthening their argument and enhancing the overall credibility of their work.
records.response_text:
Response: Thank you for the suggestion. We agree with the reviewer that this information is important. First, the exclusive use of TEM-4 writing prompts in the study was not a deliberate choice made solely for the purposes of this research. In our program, the curriculum guidelines have been iteratively updated over the years. A few years ago, students enrolled in the “Intermediate Writing” courses recommended using TEM-4 prompts for both in-class writing tasks and out-of-class practice. The main reason is that they are required to take the TEM-4 exam after completing the intermediate courses, and the TEM-4 certificate is widely recognized as a key qualification for English majors in Chinese universities. This may also be one underlying reason why we selected this course for the present study, considering the repeated measures design in the study. What we did change was introducing a more sophisticated process for selecting appropriate writing prompts, as already documented.
Second, why not use the official grading rubric? As illustrated in the figure below, the official rubric is impression-based and holistic. While this approach may be more convenient for instructors, it also carries the risk of excessive subjectivity. Moreover, since our study focuses on performance across specific dimensions of writing, such a scoring strategy is not suitable. These two considerations explain our decision to seek an alternative rubric.
Third, as illustrated in the official rubric, TEM-4 writing evaluation is essentially based on three dimensions: structure/organization, content, and language use. This justifies our adaptation of the analytical rubrics from Golparvar and Abolhasani (2022) and Zhang and Lu (2022), as both are composed of these same core scoring dimensions.
In summary, we did incorporate the official scoring criteria of TEM-4, but shifting from an impression-based and holistic approach to an analytical and dimension-based approach which suits the study better.
We want to thank the reviewer for pointing this out. In the original version, related information was only briefly introduced. We are glad to add some descriptions for these choices in the revised manuscript.

Discuss why interactive integration, rather than simply using complementary methods, promotes deeper learning and results in more meaningful and constructive feedback.
records.response_text:
Response: Thank you for the comment. We agree with the reviewer that the practical implications of the study must be clearly emphasized. We sincerely hope that this research will assist educators and researchers in implementing and designing feedback environments similar to the one we have presented. Throughout the paper we have made every effort to provide a clear and coherent account of how AF is integrated with PF to enhance learning from the literature review through Section 2.2 and into the discussion sections 4.1 and 4.2. For instance, in Sections 4.1 and 4.2, we provided detailed explanations of the results across all dimensions of feedback quality and performance improvements contextualized in the current study. Given the experimental nature of the study, this discussion offers in-depth insights into why the interactive approach to technology integration outperform the more traditional complementary approach.
However, we acknowledge that our current discussion may still be somewhat overly abstract. For example, the practical implications are grounded in concepts from previous literature (i.e., first-order and second-order scaffolding). In the following, we would also like to provide some literature-based justification (as direct response to the inquires of the reviewer here) for the reviewer only (We cannot have all the details regarding this matter in the manuscript in the full form since we are restricted by the word limit):
First, the reviewer highlighted that using PF to complement AWE feedback has been more common. We agree with the reviewer that in the body of literature, it is indeed customary for researchers to follow this trend. However, it should not be neglected that quite a few most recent studies have used AWE to complement PF. For example, in Yao et al. (2021), students used Pigai before engaging in peer feedback, in which the AWE feedback is also discussed by the peer feedback participants. Similarly, in a more recent study (Guo et al., 2024), the researcher embedded AI-based tool in the process of peer feedback as a complementary measure to improve peer feedback quality. From this aspect, we could see that, even though PF complementing AWE has been a research trend, the other way around has also been attempted. Thus, the first point we would like to argue is that the choice of using AWE as a scaffold supporting PF used in the current study is legitimate, and of course, somewhat novel. Additionally, the choice is not random or groundless, it is based on our latest understanding of feedback and our orientation towards “good feedback practices”. We will discuss the underlying theoretical insights now.
Second, in recent development and advancement in the body of literature, we have gradually shifted our understanding of feedback from a channel to provide information to a process in which students could engage and truly become proactive learners  (Winstone et al., 2022). This may be the reason why feedback practices for the formative purposes of learning, such as peer feedback and self-assessment, have become widely applied. Following this reason, when evaluating AWE feedback and peer feedback, the former is a representative of the “information transmission” model of feedback, where students receive feedback and have no chance to continuously discuss or make sense of the received feedback. In some scenarios, the feedback offered might be hard to understand or even not accurate or correct. We could no longer assume that when students received feedback, they could improve learning. On the contrary, in more interactive types of feedback practices, for example, dialogic peer feedback, the students could proactively involve in the feedback process, in which they make better sense and better use of the feedback, which is critical for learning progression. Thus, from this perspective, using AWE feedback to complement PF is not only acceptable, but also in line with our latest understanding of feedback as a process calling for (individuals’) participation, and (ideally) the collaborative interaction within a class.
Third, it is very interesting for the review to notice and inquire about the absence of teachers. In any feedback practice, it would be ideal for teachers to present, especially when the teacher involved is strong in domain knowledge and feedback literacy. However, this ideal situation doesn’t always happen. This could be attributed to the so-called “logistic issue” with traditional feedback practices. Interestingly, peer feedback and technology-based feedback has been first argued as effective alternatives to teacher feedback since it calls for less configuration of logical resources within classroom settings. The scholars used the term “new feedback paradigm” to describe the situation here: students have central role of feedback practice, widely using technology, value of feedback directly related to the interactions it elicited, with the traditional role of teachers diminished to a certain extent (de Kleijn, 2023; Jensen et al., 2023). records.comment_text: Thank you for the opportunity to review the paper titled “Metacognitive instruction to enhance EFL writers’ metacognition and revision in a GenAI-assisted feedback context”. While metacognitive instruction (MI) is not a new topic, integrating MI with GenAI-assisted feedback and prompt engineering represents an innovative direction. In this respect, the study addresses an interesting research topic. However, the major issue, at least from my perspective, is that the design and description of the intervention are difficult to follow. The first part of the intervention (i.e., the four-step sequence for strategy internalization) is acceptable, but the second part (i.e., the operationalization of a metacognitive strategy within MI) is too abstract to understand, even after several careful readings. While reading this section, numerous questions arose: How was explicit teaching of metacognitive regulation of AI feedback conducted? How was instruction on prompt engineering techniques integrated into the MI? How does the intervention guide students to set goals, monitor, and evaluate the feedback process? In this revision, we totally changed to a pedagogical perspective in presenting this section. With addition of supplementary appendix, we believe the above raised question can be answered with greater detail of information on the instructional content and process.
A question we would like to explicitly answer is the effects of the MI. As can be found in this revised version, teaching of prompt engineering skills was not standalone in our practice, it is used as a “practical layer” to enable the teaching of metacognition in an AI-assisted context. Therefore, the observed effects can be seen as the outcome of the overall intervention itself instead a simple combination of traditional MI + prompt engineering. records.comment_text: 9. “Person variable” refers to the learners’ self-perception or whether they are equivalent to endowing an AI with a personality. This confusion should be clarified or corrected to maintain the integrity of the theory.
records.response_text:
Response: Thank you for your comment. It’s apparent that, in this study, we inherited the traditional definition of “person variable” in conceptualization, however, we also extended to include students’ abilities to setting AI with specific persona as an AI-human collaborative form of “person knowledge” (can be seen from Appendix S3 and the part the reviewer is referring to).
This is not a taken-for-granted effort nor totally groundless. According to Singh and Muis (2024), in a collaborative setting, metacognitive knowledge would extend beyond individual level to include “knowledge of self and others based on a history of experiences” (p. 180). In their framework, metacognitive knowledge includes both the more traditional person-level conditions (self-perceptions) and Person x Group-level conditions (perceptions about the partner, collaborator, group members, etc.).
Following this path, our original understanding is that, during human-GenAI feedback interactions, setting AI with a specific persona requires students’ knowledge of their own learning capabilities, limitations, as well as possible AI strength to serve as a supportive partner. This led to our decision to classify the “persona”-related behaviors or understanding into the category of “person variable”.
However, extending the concept to a more collaborative scope requires extra efforts to re-frame the core concept within metacognition frameworks. After careful re-consideration, we decided to stick to the original conceptualization of metacognitive knowledge in the current study. Such extension has its own merit, but it would add extra content to the study, which might further confuse the readers. Thus, we have made corresponding revision in the discussion, to limit our interpretation on person variable within well-established theoretical frameworks.
Finally, we still want to thank the reviewer for this very significant comment. We wish we can seize opportunity to have the content of this paper easy to follow and rigorous according to definition in the literature review. At the same time, we also feel that traditional concepts, such as metacognitive knowledge, might need reconsideration in the era of human-AI collaborative learning. This might be a good topic for future inquiries.

records.comment_text:
Dear Prof. Lee,
Thanks for being the editor of the manuscript entitled Development of feedback seeking abilities of L2 writers using ChatGPT: a mixed method multiple case study (TAPE-D-23-01143), which is currently under the consideration of The Asia-Pacific Education Researcher (TAPER).
I would like to extend the warmest thanks to you and both reviewers for the valuable comments and constructive suggestions. The manuscript has been revised in accordance with these comments. Changes made are described as follows in boxes. Correspondingly, all relevant amendments made in the revision are marked with color yellow (for comments from reviewer#1) and green (reviewer#2) in the manuscript.
Introduction
1.The definition of feedback-seeking abilities is not identified in the "Introduction", and this notion is not distinguished from feedback-seeking behaviors. No explanation may leave readers thoroughly perplexed. It is recommended to introduce feedback seeking abotiles in this section.
records.response_text:
Response: Thank you for the comment. In developing the present study, the term feedback seeking behavior is used to represent the “process” in which students utilize feedback seeking abilities to ask ChatGPT to generate useful information (feedback). I agree with the reviewer that in the introduction, the term feedback seeking ability is not clearly defined and introduced, thus causing potential confusion for the readers. Hence, in the revision, I have explicitly defined and separated the two terms (as follows). 
In conventional L2 settings, learners’ agentic feedback acquisition is defined as feedback seeking behavior (FSB), learners’ inquiry and monitoring of received feedback from teachers or peers (Papi et al., 2019). Alternatively, learners in ChatGPT-enhanced environments must possess feedback seeking abilities, the skills to strategically use prompting techniques enabling ChatGPT to generate efficient feedback for specific tasks.
2.Research on ChatGPT and related learning behaviors (e.g., information seeking, self-regulation) has been published. Authors are expected to include these highly related references in the Introduction.
Response: Thanks for this suggestion. I appreciate the reviewers’ suggestions for including some relevant research on learning behaviors in the context of ChatGPT-enhanced learning. When I was originally writing the manuscript, such studies were neglected or not published yet. Reference to such studies would help frame the knowledge gap in examining students’ feedback seeking behaviors in the new learning environment. Hence two studies were added to the second paragraph of the introduction. Please kindly refer to the revised introduction.
3.It can be necessary to at least briefly articulate the relationship between the two research questions, and elaborate on the importance of these two research questions. Through the section "Introduction". I felt that the authors did not prepare the readers for the close connection between these two research questions.
Response: Thanks for the suggestions. I agree that the internal connections between the two RQs should be shown to the readers. I tried to combine the present comment with the last comment for literature review (comment #4 in LR) since they share a similar problem. Consequently, I added a short section of “The current study” at the end of the literature review, trying to provide the underlying rationale for the study and the reasons to raise the two specific RQs. Correspondingly, the RQs are moved to that section as well. Please kindly refer to the revision for changes taken to address the two comments.
Literature Review
1.P.4 Please offer a more detailed account of "the settings of existing studies on FSB contradict the emerging learning environment in which the role of technologies have been elevated significantly", especially how existing studies on FSB contradict the technology- or AI- mediated feedback information.
Response: Thanks for pointing it out. In the original writing, the existing body of literature on L2 learners’ FSB were minimal. Hence, the contrast here (existing research vs. the need to carry out a new study to study students’ FSB in the context of ChatGPT, which significantly differs from the old settings) were not clearly framed. In the revision (also in response to the comment from another reviewer), previous studies were added in greater detail. Correspondingly, the gap (changing setting caused by GAI, typically ChatGPT) is elucidated. Additionally, I also tried to avoid using words such as “contradict” in the revision as an effort to dial down the tone as if the present study is going to totally reject the existing perspectives on FSB. In the revision, I used Jensen et al. (2023) definition of new feedback paradigm as a guidance to separate the present study from existing studies on FSB in L2 pedagogy. Please refer to the revised paragraph (in yellow.)
2.P.5 "Nevertheless, to the best of my knowledge, there is no available investigation into the effects of ChatGPT as an AWCF provider in authentic pedagogical settings. Furthermore, students' involvement and learning behaviors in eliciting, evaluating, and utilizing the feedback provided by ChatGPT remain unstudied", a lack of research is not a good rationale for conducting this study. It is recommended to explain the differences between ChatGPT and other AWCF.
Response: Thanks for this comment. I agree with the reviewer that “no prior research” contribute to the novelty of the study but not a good rationale to support it. The actual rationale of the study originated from both ChatGPT’s potential as corrective feedback provider as well as the changes in learning behavior it would cause. The original writing focused on the former and largely neglected the latter. To revise, I have added a few arguments on the changes in learning behavior and the functions of AWCF in the context of ChatGPT. Basically, compared to traditional AWCF systems, ChatGPT: 1) rely on human-machine communication and is capable of providing individualized feedback; 2) is powerful to provide feedback on a large range of evaluative constructs or linguistics features; and 3) could gradually provide feedback with better quality after multiple turns of prompting-and-responding.
As a result, the added contents are as follows: 
Furthermore, ChatGPT brings changes to L2 learning behaviors in seeking and utilizing (corrective) feedback. First, the human-ChatGPT communication is bi-directional, making ChatGPT a learner-aware and human-like feedback provider (Barrot, 2023). Second, when properly prompted, ChatGPT could be utilized to feedback on a wide range of writing constructs and linguistic features, inclusive but not limited to grammar and syntactical correctness (Mizumoto & Eguchi, 2023). Third, multi-turn human-ChatGPT communication is encouraged and corroborated to be conducive to performance improvement of ChatGPT-generated feedback (Bang et al., 2023). Given the human-AI communication mechanism and corresponding changes in learning behaviors, relevant studies from the learners’ perspectives are urgently needed.
3.It is recommended to review the previous studies of ChatGPT on L2 learning and L2 writing in this section.
Response: Thanks for this comment. At the time of the original writing (a few months ago), there were nearly no published works on ChatGPT and L2 learning/writing. During the recent months, a few empirical studies have been published. Hence, I see it as a good opportunity for the present study to catch up with the latest development in the field. However, to date, such studies remain limited in number (excluding quite a few of opinion ones). Again I would like to thank the reviewer for such comment, which makes the review of literature complete and comprehensive, to a certain degree.

Please refer to the added review of literature as follows:
Since its debut, researchers have attempted to investigate into ChatGPT’s effects on L2 writing. Yan (2023) explored L2 writers’ abilities to utilize ChatGPT’s text generation functionality in writing and their perceptions towards the potential threats to academic integrity. Barrot (2023) summarized advantages and pitfalls of ChatGPT’s potential usage in L2 writing classrooms, as well as a few recommendations for L2 teachers. Furthermore, efforts have been made to incorporate ChatGPT in L2 writing assessment. Mizumoto and Eguchi (2023) reported convincing accuracy and reliability from the automated scoring on L2 writing products by ChatGPT.
4.At the end of your literature review, it would be very helpful to add a brief "research purpose" section that summarizes the existing research and reminds the reader of the innovation and purpose of the present study.
Response: Thanks for pointing this out. As stated in previous responses, I have combined the rationale/purpose of the study and the reasons to raise the two RQs in an added section of “the current study”. Please refer to the added section for more details.
Methods
1.Feedback seeking strategies, feedback seeking behaviors and feedback seeking abilities seem interchangeably used. It is suggested to use the term feedback seeking abilities in this and the following sections.
Response: Thanks for this suggestion. This is utterly important. In the revised writing, the term feedback seeking abilities is consistently used.
2.P.8, it is recommended to provide more details about how to assess the three participants' writing proficiencies and technological competencies, and why assess their writing proficiency and technological competencies.
Response: Thanks for the comment. Though students’ writing proficiency and technological competencies were not used in latter part of the paper, they were critical in recruiting samples and forming the cases. During the revision, the measurements of writing proficiencies and technological competencies were added through two footnotes. In addition, the rationale for such measurement was appended to the main text. Please refer to the changes in the manuscript.
3.Readers may be curious about the uneven gender distribution of participants.
Response: Thanks for raising this very interesting question. On the one hand, out of gender equality, gender distribution is not a concern during the participant recruitment processes. On the other hand, our population (L2 writers learning in the program) showcased a gender ration of 1.8:1 (female: male), making the current gender distribution of the case study rationale and acceptable. With this said, I personally would argue that gender issue is not a major concern for the present study and I have no pre-determined hypothesis about the correlation between gender and feedback seeking abilities in the context of ChatGPT.
Results
1.I thought the content and macro-organization of your discussion was clear. Still, in this section, it is recommended to organize this section in alignment with two research questions, that is, RQ1: What characterizes the development of feedback seeking abilities of the participants in the interaction with ChatGPT for feedback? RQ2: What factors (if any) influence the development of feedback seeking abilities of L2 writers?
Response: Thanks for the advice. I agree with the reviewer that such heading would make the results presentation clearer and easier to comprehend for the readers. In the revision, the headings are changed accordingly. 
Additionally, I have taken one step back in framing RQ2 from “influential factors” to “perceptions of” development of feedback seeking abilities. In doing so, RQ2 are more general and include not only the decisive factors but also students’ general perceptions. Hence, the RQ could better capture all the contents emerged from the interview.
2.While I appreciate the use of quotes to clarify "Factors for the development of feedback seeking abilities", it is recommended to add quotes in the section "Wrap-up of individual learning experiences".
Response: Thanks for the advice. However, during the revision. I have found the original “wrap-up of individual learning experiences” less relevant to the RQ2. Hence, I tried to remove the subsection. I sincerely appreciate the reviewer’s suggestion all the same.
Discussion
1.Authors argue that "Students with higher language proficiency tended to create content-rich prompts in relatively fewer rounds of interaction with AI system, while students with moderate language proficiency resorted to an opposite path". However, the authors did not clearly provide information of which students have high-, moderate-, and low proficiency, and did not offer information about methods dividing students into three language proficiencies.
Response: Thanks for this comment. The issue here is important, particularly for a case study. With limited number of participants, it is not easy for the researcher to generalize the findings. The three participants, albeit different in individual characteristics, could not perfectly represent high-, mid-, and low-achievers (particularly language proficiencies). Instead of defining explicitly that each participant can represent a certain group of students, I would choose not to over-generalize the findings. Hence, the findings are to be discussed in a more measured fashion, particularly the generalizability of the data. 
To fix the issue, I resorted to the following measures: 1) explicitly stating the cohort of students the participants respectively represented in the “participant” section; 2) append actual cases (i.e., the three participants) to the expression of “high achievers” etc., in the discussion; and 3) add generalizability concerns to the limitations of the study. 
The reviewer is invited to check the changes taken (scattered in methodology, discussion, and conclusion sections of the paper). Hopefully the combination of the above three strategies could yield a better discussion of the results from the present case study. 
The three cases stand for three groups of students: 
Based on students’ performance in pre-project language assessments and teachers’ recommendations, Toby represents those with high language proficiency and technological competence; Lisa stands for those with mid-low language proficiency and high technological competence; and Isabella exemplifies those with high language proficiency and mid-low technological competence.
2.P.20, while two feedbacking behaviors (inquiry and monitoring) and two feedback seeking abilities (elicitation and refinement strategies) are compared in this section, readers may still be puzzled about their differences. It is recommended to discuss in depth two feedback seeking abilities and their differences from FSB with reference to the results of this study.
Response: Thanks for the comment. In the first place, I agree with the reviewer that a clear and explicit discussion comparing the obtained finding against existing knowledge of FSB is mandatory for the present study. Upon reflection, I confess that the current way (having the comparison in discussing RQ2 but lacking detail) is not effective. 
Additionally, the way such comparison is presented may leave reader a false impression that the study did not respect the insights and knowledge from previous studies. Contrarily, the point that should be underlined is that the differences in the understanding of feedback seeking in different settings originated from the changing learning environment. For the better development of education with the enhancement from technology, traditional pedagogical insights should be respected, uplifted, and further developed. 
Hence, I have made moved all the relevant comparison against FSB insights into a new paragraph that follows the present one. Hopefully, the comparison between the findings emerged from the present study and FSB (particularly Papi et al. (2019) could be established in a more direct and comprehensive fashion. Additionally, this could also make the discussion of RQ2 more focused and easier to understand. Please check the changes taken in relevant parts (marked in yellow).
Conclusion
1.The conceptual and pedagogical implications are too general. Please clarify more on how results indicate these implications.
Response: Thanks for the comments. I agree with the reviewer that the original implication was written in an unsatisfactory manner. Additionally, with the revision, the implication could be enriched and specified. Hence, the implication is rewritten as follows:
The study delivered conceptual and pedagogical implications. First, a sociomaterial and ecological perspective towards feedback would trigger researchers to expand and redevelop existing conceptualization in the field of instructional feedback. The study revealed that ChatGPT, when actively and strategically utilized, offered a competitive solution for AWCF in L2 learning. Considering the growth in the application of AI, such domain-specific and in-depth investigations into the provision and utilization of feedback in innovative learning environments would be helpful for the sustained development of educational studies in the new era. Second, educators should consider the development of students’ abilities to use state-of-the-art tools. The results showed that the quality and effectiveness of ChatGPT-generated feedback were closely related to students’ feedback seeking abilities. However, to date, such abilities were understudied, let alone properly trained. There remained much to be done for educators, e.g., altering curriculum and assessment setups, (re)constructing a learning environment levering AI affordance and peer collaboration, providing training on AI skills, etc.

The review in this section needs also to prepare your readers for the potential differences in the TS, TPS and PS conditions. Currently the logic in this section is not very clear.
Response: Thanks for the comment. In the original writing, I guess I have tried too hard to construct the theoretical framework from relevant theories. Based on the reviewers’ comment, the outcomes are not as expected. Additionally, seeking a theoretical intersection among so many theories are challenging for both the author and the readers. To improve, I have focused on two aspects in the revision: (1) theoretical underpinnings to support the (feasibility and effect) of collaborative processing of ChatGPT-generated AF; and (2) potential approaches to collaborative processing of such AF, particularly why we need to add new insights about the role played by teachers, given the fact that previous literature has informed us that peer scaffolding could be effective in promoting the uptake of feedback and writing improvement. Hopefully, the revised version could be reader-friendlier and inform readers with needed backgrounds of the study.
Method

Response: Thanks for the question. Students’ interest is measured by a self-reported survey. Teacher’s recommendation was used as a supplementary source to identify students who are keen and appropriate as participants. 
Yes, they are from different classes, but same grade (sophomores). 
In practice, only students with outstanding engagement and interest in the project are recruited. Since the study is a pioneering effort to examine the impact of ChatGPT in an experimental setting, the researcher expected that the participants should be in possession of higher level of L2 abilities and willingness and interest to continue the exploration of using ChatGPT as a potential AF provider for writing improvement and learning progression. Hence, I have added that:
Only students with adequate L2 proficiency and outstanding interest in the project were recruited since the study would call for a relatively higher level of language proficiency and engagement with ChatGPT.
What kind of “in-class scaffolding and guidance” provided by the teachers? How could they judge when students faced challenges and difficulties?
Response: Thanks for the inquiries. In the revision, I have added that the content of teachers’ training as follows: 
The training focused on: (1) strategies to use ChatGPT for AF; and (2) suggested ways to offer scaffolding to the students. Noticeably, the author has put sufficient energy to train the teachers to use standard ways in using and assisting students’ usage of ChatGPT (e.g., how to teach students to use a standard and replicable workflow of using ChatGPT, and how to prepare and provide modelling on the usage of ChatGPT) in L2 writing classrooms.

Accordingly, the following has been added in relevant part to descript the contents of teachers’ scaffolding: 

The teachers were trained to use the following strategies for the scaffolding: (1) using modelling to offer assistance for the whole class; and (2) responding to students’ call for help during the writing and revision processes; and (3) replying to students’ inquiries through real-time communication platforms (e.g., WeChat, Tencent meeting). The foci of teachers’ scaffolding were: (1) strategies to further prompt ChatGPT for clarification and improvement of feedback; (2) suggested ways to appreciate and potentially apply the AF messages; and (3) appropriate approaches to validate and rectify the AF messages if ambiguities and false information were identified.

In practice, the teachers are required to impart what they have received from their training as scaffolding and assistance to the students. In the two groups with teacher involvement (i.e., TS and TPS), 6 teachers worked with the students (individual or peer). Take the TS group for example, each teacher could watch the learning situations of about 5 students. The teacher could identify students’ encounter of difficulties through : (1) students’ active reporting: the students could either raise hand or send online messages to let the teacher know they have faced difficulties; and (2) based on their own observation, for example, if a students hesitate to make any progress for a relatively long period of time in class, the teacher would actively ask if he or she is facing some challenges. In the study itself, based on my own observation as researcher, most students were active and engaged with interest. Hence, the chances for students to actively report issues in need of assistance were rather high and even higher than expected. The reason might be that the outcomes of the study could be used by the students as components of their semester grades as well as the democratic, fun, and engaging atmosphere we have strived to create.
Why did you ask students to a uniform ChatGPT prompting? How does that reflect ‘authentic writing context’? Were students restricted in follow-up conversations with ChatGPT to discuss the feedback?
Response: Thanks for the inquiries about the uniform prompting strategy used in the study. The reason to use such a prompting strategy is that ChatGPT excels in responding in an information-rich “context” (support from previous studies is listed in the paper). To help student using ChatGPT, we ask them to prompt the AI system in a more information-rich and detailed way. 
This doesn’t collide with the “authentic writing context” of the study. It is a recommend way to use ChatGPT, not a manipulation that would hinder or limit students’ usage of the AI system for learning progression.
For example, without any training or assistance, the students would be likely to simply prompt ChatGPT with questions like “can you give my work a mark out of 100?”. Comparatively, offering assessment criteria and desired scope for the evaluation would possibly make ChatGPT’s answer more useful and aligned with our expectations. 
Finally, students are not only allowed to iteratively and incrementally use ChatGPT, but also encouraged to do it in a multi-turn fashion (once again, supported by previous studies). 
In the revision, relevant information has been appended to this section.
Need more information on how different feedback conditions were implemented. Whose writing did TS, TPS and PS group collaboratively seek feedback from ChatGPT? How did they do the revisions (collaborative piece first and then their individual piece?)? For TPS and PS group, if students are already collaborating with other agents (what do you mean by ‘agents’ any way?) to co-process the feedback from ChatGPT, what peer learners are added in these two groups? Are you simply testing whether the amount of peers involved in the co-meaning making of the feedback matter through the PS and TPS group? Also, what is the difference between TS and TPS groups (simply the amount of peers involved?)?? In Table 2, you seem to indicate that students work with feedback from ChatGPT collaboratively for TS, TPS and PS groups? But then in the following text, you seem to indicate that TS group worked with the feedback from ChatGPT individually?
Response: Thanks for the inquiries on the details. I will respond one by one.
To begin with, the term “agent” is used to refer to “people involved in scenarios with assessment and feedback”. Please refer to literature such as Panadero and Lipnevich (2022). I have attached a simple screenshot from the paper FYI.
Second, regarding the processes involved in writing and revision. It should be noticed that the draft writing and revision processes are always individual. The collaborative processing of feedback only took place after the drafting and before the revision. In latter part of this response letter, I have also answered this with greater detail. 
Third, TPS = group with teacher and peer scaffolding; PS = group with peer scaffolding, here agent means those who offered scaffolding. I think after the clarification of the definition of the term “agent”, the details of the conditions are clarified. 
Fourth, regarding the differences between TS and TPS, the differences are not only the involvement of teacher vs teacher + peers. It is a matter of the scale of feedback processing. For the TPS group, the individual writers could seek scaffolding from a 2-layer structure: (1) the writer could discuss with peer about minute details related to the feedback, the sociocultural discussion between them could solve most of the simpler issues with received feedback; (2) if they still have issues with the feedback (after the peer-based discussion), they could resort to the teachers for help. Traditionally, we believe that L2 teachers (MKO from the perspective of sociocultural learning theory) are likely to make better use of feedback messages due to their higher level of domain knowledge, and experiences. That’s the most distinct differences between the multiple conditions used in the study. 
Finally, TS group didn’t work with the feedback individually, they were scaffolded by the teacher.
Also for the TS and TPS groups, teachers ‘provided face-to-face and on-demand scaffolding on feedback seeking strategies’. So it’s possible that students did not take advantage of the scaffolding from teachers at all? If so, how is it different from the IP group or PS group? Also, what do you mean by ‘feedback seeking strategies’? any example? Why feedback seeking strategies only? Did they help with the interpretation of the feedback and actions based on the feedback? The PS and TPS groups completed their tasks inside the lab too? For the groups that involved peers, do they also give ‘feedback seeking strategies’ as in the TS condition? What’s the rationale of asking peer collaborations via technological platforms. Were the web-based collaborative writing platforms used in synchronously or asynchronously?
Response: Thanks for the inquiries on the details. I will respond one by one. 
First, it is theoretically possible that the participant under a certain condition totally refused the intervention. But the study has certain measures to avoid such occurrences. For example, in the sampling phase, we have selected those who are interested in making effective usage of AI. Hence, the students involved in the study are less likely to refuse potential improvement to use the AI tool. Additionally, we have a measure to enhance students’ engagement in the study (i.e., the grades of the writing tasks would be used as scores for assignments in the writing course, which will eventually become part of their semester grades for the course). Therefore, it is less likely that the students in the T* groups will totally ignore the scaffolding from the teachers. In simple words, I think we could only try to beat down the chances but not possible to totally avoid the chances for the mentioned cases to happen.
Second. Why feedback seeking strategies? Since feedback seeking matters in using GAI. GAI could be seen as an intelligent chatbot. Hence, the abilities to elicit it into responding in the desired or optimal manner matters. 
Third, the scaffolding is not limited to strategies only. The reviewer is advised to pay attention to Table 2, in which the contents of the scaffolding are listed in detail. However, I do found inconsistencies between the text of the paper and the table. I have omitted other elements of scaffolding in the main text. To rectify, I have added them accordingly. To sum, the scaffolding includes not only strategies to elicit feedback, but how to interpret them, and (if needed) the strategies to re-elicit ChatGPT for improved feedback, etc. 
Finally, technological-based platform facilities communication and is also traceable if the writer needs to review their previous discussion during revision. In the study, both asynchronous and synchronous communication channels were used out of the consideration that the writers might need different communicative approaches in the face of different situations. For example, for very simple issues, they might need to ask for a yes/no response from peer/teacher. While in the face of challenging issues, possibly a situation in need of re-elicit ChatGPT to totally reframe its responses for feedback, a thread discussion on the collaborative platforms might be more helpful. 

The relevant part has been revised with greater details. The reviewer is invited to review such parts for reference.
Need more information on what the training on ChatGPT’s usage involved. What were the self-paced practicing about?
Response: Thanks for the comment. As for the training of teachers, I have added the following details:
The training focused on: (1) strategies to use ChatGPT for AF; and (2) suggested ways to offer scaffolding to the students. Noticeably, the author has put sufficient energy to train the teachers to use standard ways in using and assisting students’ usage of ChatGPT (e.g., how to teach students to use a standard and replicable workflow of using ChatGPT, and how to prepare and provide modelling on the usage of ChatGPT) in L2 writing classrooms.
In the training sessions provided to the students, the teachers simply tried to impart what they have been trained to the students in addition to their own experiences and understandings. Hence, the content of the training for students could be understood as an inheritance from what the teachers have received during their own training by the author (see above).
Furthermore, a key aspect of ChatGPT’s usage is how to effectively prompt the AI system:
In the training sessions, recommend ways to design feedback requirement and rating criteria have been displayed.
As for the self-paced sessions, students are offered freedom to decide how and what to practice. However, the teachers gave them some instructions to perform, for example: 
For example, the students were required to replicate the modelling examples teachers have showed them during the training sessions.
For T1, T2 and T3, were the writing on the same topic? For the three tasks, did they spend one session write up the article and one session work on revision based on the feedback from ChatGPT? How long were each session? Did they finish one writing task each week after the learning weeks?  How were the topic(s) different from or similar to the new topic three weeks later?
Response: Thanks for the inquiry. All students write on the same topic for a given task. They are advised to use 1 session for drafting, 2 sessions for feedback seeking and processing, and 1 session for revision. In the Chinese context, a session lasts for 45 minutes. The topic for NT was also selected from official CET-6 test compilations, hence, it is of the same requirement and difficulties, but with a different topic. 
Above info, if not mentioned in the original submission, is added in the revision.
Altogether how many writings did the students produce over the span of seven weeks?
Response: Thanks for the inquiry. Over the span of 7 weeks, students actually finished 5 writing tasks. However, only the three mentioned in the study are collected as data. The other two are only for instructional purposes (Don’t forget there is a writing course going on).
From another angle, the three tasks completed by the participants were used as assignments in the course as well. 
Hence, in simpler terms, the research project is embedded in the course. But only the data mentioned in the study are collected and used for analytical purposes.
What is the rationale of spreading the three Tasks in week 2, 5 and 7?
Response: Thanks for the inquiry. It is purposeful design for longitudinal study (or a repeated measures study) so that the developmental trajectories made by the students could be analyzed. For example, the information Figure 5 provided to us would not be possible if the students were only measure once in the study (frequently occurred in studies employing a one-off interventional design). Additionally, the selection of week 2, 5, and 7 was purposeful: offer them some time to reflect upon the knowledge gains received from previous round of task completion.
How did you calculate the L2 writing learning? From your current description, it’s not clear exactly how it was calculated.
Response: Thanks for the inquiry. In the present study, I tried to use two terminologies for the two different perspectives towards learning. (i.e., “task improvement” and “learning”). The main reason to use these terms is that “task improvement” refers to the improvement made by students after using AF for revision whereas “learning” refers to students’ abilities to draft on their own without using AF for assistance. From a theoretical perspective, such division of the two statuses in writing learning echoed Wiliam (2018) conceptualization of “performance” and “learning”. According to Wiliam (2018), the effectiveness of a certain instructional intervention is justified if it could be used to promote learning instead of merely performance. From my own standpoint, I attribute the two terminologies I used here as a situated interpretation of Wiliam’s (2018). 
In previous literature, such viewpoints are also shared by other researchers. For example, the reviewer is advised to check “The influence of three approaches to feedback on L2 writing task improvement and subsequent learning” a https://doi.org/10.1016/j.stueduc.2023.101291, which shared the similar disciplinary and contextual background with the present study. According to the authors, the division of “task improvement” and “subsequent learning” offered a chance to observe the impact of feedback from a learning-oriented perspective and is supported by previous theories such as Wiliam (2018).
I would invite the review to pay attention to the paragraph before framing the research questions, the above justification on variable selection has already been made:
Situated in the context of L2 writing pedagogy, the study measures and investigates learning outcomes dyadically as during-intervention L2 writing task improvement (i.e., the improvement students made after using ChatGPT-generated AF between draft and final writing artifact scores during the intervention) and progression in subsequent learning processes (i.e., the progression students made in draft scores during and after the intervention).
How did you ensure that the difficulty and familiarity levels are similar across the tasks and the NT for the four groups?
Response: Thanks for asking about it. 
As for difficulties, the researcher conducted a pre-study assessment using a panel of co-researchers who are also teachers at the research site to select writing tasks from the official compilation. Based on a three-round selection, the current three topic were selected because the panel members perceived that they are on a similar level of difficulties. I have reported such process in the methodology section in the revision.  
As for topic familiarity, no such measurement was carried out because, students are familiar with the topics of CET6, which is a nation-level exam. (on a side not, in the Chinese L2 context, passing the CET-4/6 exams before graduation has been a common goal for college students, so most of the students have investigated sufficient time and energy to the preparation of the exams). From a researcher perspective, since topic familiarity should not a concern and it is not a major variable in the present study, I would choose to keep it invisible for fear that additional complexity would hamper readers’ comprehension.
Discussion
You explanations on the observed better performance among the control group need to be supported with the examination of the nature of the interaction with ChatGPT. Your current explanations were based on hypothetical discussions. Since you do have students’ interaction data with ChatGPT, why didn’t you use the differences in the nature of the interaction and the revision adoption patterns across the different groups as evidence to support your analysis?
AND
For the TS and TPS conditions, do you have the data on how much support did these two groups receive from the teachers? i.e., did you check on the validity of the TS and TPS conditions?
Response: Thanks for the two comment. As stated, I regret since I believe it would be not possible to implement the suggested amendment although the suggestions were valuable and merit extra paths to enhance the analytical procedures in the present study.

Other than this, I have tried to change my tones in the discussion sections. Particularly those sounds too hypothetical. For example, in discussion the results pertinent to RQ1, instead of inferring, I tried to raise concerns related to the blind usage of ChatGPT-generated AF. I think it does improve the criticality and objectivity of the discussion section.
Once again, I would thank the reviewer. Although I didn’t incorporate the suggested changes, I firmly believe this is the direction to continuously explore the topic we have made in this paper. The contents, strategies, and patterns of the scaffolding as well as human-AI, and peer interactions are all the good topics and directions worth digging, if we acknowledge the impact and potential of GAI in language education.
For the TS, PS and TPS conditions, were students’ drafts and final papers individual work or collaborative work? Based on your description, it seems to be a collaborative piece. If so, what you examined might not so much on collaborative processing of feedback, but rather the effects of collaborative writing on writing development.
Response: Thanks for the comment. In the present study, the collaboration, regardless teacher-student or peer-based, is limited to the processing of AF. According to the understanding of the cognitive processes involved in L2 writing, for example those of Shintani and Aubrey (2016), the revision process involved four steps: 1) noting the errors/correction; 2) comparing the text; 3) making decision; and 4) executing the revision. In the present study, the “processing of feedback” is only limited to the first three steps. Hence, the final steps (revision execution) are carried out by the writers themselves along. From this point of view, I would argue that the draft and final writing artifacts were both individual instead of collaborative work. 
From another perspective, the notion of “collaborative processing of feedback” has been used in studies where the finalization of the writing artifacts was a peer-based activities such as Mujtaba et al. (2021). Following this line of reasoning, the doubts that the study is actually an investigation into collaborative writing instead of “collaborative processing of feedback” should not be a major concern. Anyhow, since the present study has severed the revision execution and feedback processing processes, there should be no reason to have such doubts. 
I think there is some ambiguities in explicitly introducing the above procedures. To rectify, I have added details in the procedure section so that readers could understand that we have kept the revision finalization processes to the writer themselves.
How do you explain greater improvement in task performance but not in writing learning among the IP group? How can you rule out the potential effect of topic familiarity of the writing task?
Response: Thanks for the inquiries here about the IP group. Personally speaking, I think the inabilities of the IP group to transform what they have reaped from AI during task improvement to subsequent learning processes was a key aspect worth delving into. 
In the discussion (after revision based on another reviewer’s suggestions), I have explained the phenomenon from a threefold perspective: 
1). the remarkable task improvement itself justified the power of ChatGPT as a useful tool to significantly evaluate and improve writing artifacts in L2 settings; 
2). the inabilities as mentioned above would trigger our concerns about the potential random and blind use of ChatGPT. Although students could make their writing much better with the help of the tools, but the process did not successfully elicit “inner feedback” and ultimately leading to less improvement in the development of L2 writing abilities. 
3). Comparatively, the other groups showed a more controlled and crucial use of AF, which would facilitate the development of L2 writing abilities and effective uptake of AF. 
Based on the above points, I would argue that the phenomenon itself is well explained in the discussion section. 

Regarding the issue mentioned by the reviewer about topic familiarity. I would explain as follows: 
1). Although topic familiarity is not a major variable considered in the present paper, it should not be a major concern because CET6 is a nation-level exam in the context of China, with which all the L2 learners at college level are very familiar. Additionally, the writing test is generally on “hot” or popular topics in the Chinese society. Hence the students would have a similar level of topic familiarity with the writing task. 
2). The methodological design of the present study would effectively control the potential bias caused by various level of topic familiarity among the students. The study adopted a longitudinal and repeated-measures design. Therefore, it is not possible for the IP group to benefit from familiarity with all the three writing tasks consistently throughout the research. 
However, I do appreciate the reviewer’s mentioning of the variable of topic familiarity. Being an initial attempt to explore the impact of the practices to use ChatGPT in L2 writing classrooms, I believe it is understandable for the present study to not include other variables such as topic familiarity. In subsequent studies, the role played by such variables in the new setting could be explored. I would thank the reviewer again for highlighting the landscape ahead of us at present stage.
The discussion may need to link back to the theoretical framework to discuss the observed differences in the individual and collaborative conditions & different collaborative conditions (the TS and TPS condition and the PS condition).
Response: Thanks for the comment. I agree with the reviewer that a stronger link to the theoretical framework would be helpful in enhancing the theoretical value of the discussion section as well as the overall writing. 
To improve, I paid sufficient attention to a few aspects of the framework, particularly the comparison between the two major modes of feedback processing (i.e., sociomaterial vs. sociomaterial+ sociocultural approaches). Additionally, since a more minimalistic theoretical framework was used in the revision to support the study, it makes easier for the author to interpret the results against the framework. Hopefully, the revised version could contribute more to the theoretical insights we have for the processing of (automated) feedback in the field of L2 pedagogy.

A GENERAL response: Thanks for the detailed comments from Reviewer #3, particularly on the theoretical underpinnings and the corresponding lenses from which the discussion of results is framed. I chose a relatively minimalistic approach to solve the issues. Since interactional data were not included and the study itself focused on the effects of different feedback processing modes on the short-term and long-term effects of writing development, I would like to restructure relevant parts of the paper to focus on its own scope. Therefore, we have conducted multiple individual studies to focus on different aspect of the whole issue. To date, some of the findings have been published and some are still on their way. It’s very natural for the main researcher, which is me, to explicitly use some interaction-related theories while designing the current study, which is actually one of the major aims of the whole research project. Now, I fully agree with the reviewer that, for academic rigor and consistency, the current paper should be somewhat restructured so that we would not puzzle our readers, and let the current paper do its own job and nothing more. 
Finally, I still want to thank the reviewer’s suggestions since it could deliver more merit to the current work and the whole research project. records.comment_text: 5) To what extent does the GenAI PF prompts address the three assessment criteria (content, organisation, language?) This would help with assessment validity in light of the PF intervention.
records.response_text:
Response: Thanks for this inquiry. We are delighted to explain as follows.
In the current work, we utilized GenAI to enhance student generated PF. Therefore, it is purposefully designed not to evaluate the writing performance directly. This is similar to the feedback model in Guo et al. (2024). As illustrated in the following figure on the lefthand side, GenAI offers “feedback on (student-generated) PF comments”. So, the comment provided by GenAI is expected to be about the “quality of the PF comment” instead of “quality of students’ writing product”. Feedback-on-feedback (also known as back evaluation in some other literature) has been a core phase within dialogic PF processes (can be seen from the dialogic PF model of Zhao et al.(2024), which is shown in the following figure on the right hand side). By doing so, we placed GenAI as a “assistant helping student improving PF” rather than “a tool helping student get alternative evaluation from a machine”. This choice echoes the student-centered perspectives towards GenAI usage in assessment (as shown in the updated GenAI policy session). With this model, we keep the role of providing original PF comment on writing in the hand of the students. To help them provide good, actionable, and criteria-referenced PF comment, we offered them a grading rubric (which include the three dimensions of writing performance in this study: content, organization, and language use). Therefore, the original PF comment is already based on the three dimensions, while GenAI is utilized to give additional enhancement so that the PF comments could be better in “feedback quality”. Based on previous research (e.g., Fraile et al., 2023; Wang, 2014; Yan, 2024), offering rubric as a supportive tool could effectively enhance the quality of feedback in formative assessment. This explains why we didn’t provide a performance rubric in the prompting template, but instead a PF quality rubric was included in the template.
Hence, the effect of GenAI enhancement on writing performance (especially the three criteria-based dimensions) is somewhat indirect, unlike other studies where technology-based feedback comment was directly applied by the students for revision without enabling students to reflect, discuss, and transform the feedback comment. Here we visualize the above point below:
As illustrated, this approach included two phases: first, GenAI is incorporated in the traditional peer-based feedback processes so that student-generated PF comment could be improved with technological enhancement; then, with the improved PF comment, student can then apply it to revise their draft to a (presumably) higher standard so that writing performance improvement is achieved. This mechanism is actually in tandem with the Nicol and Macfarlane-Dick (2006) model. Specifically, the feedback intervention first affects an internally observable outcome (quality of the PF comment), this outcome is internal to students’ learning process, which helps generate effective “internal feedback” which could eventually affect learning itself; then the above effect is transferred to impact an “externally observable outcome”, which is the writing performance within the current work. 
With the above stated, we might be able to conclude that, the study, which follows a tri-functional perspective on feedback to evaluate the innovative approach’s overall impact on learning, was keen on the outer box (intervention → externally observable outcomes). We believe the work has offered sufficient insights in this regard. However, the study didn’t provide a direct observation on the inner box (intervention → internally observable outcomes). We believe it is a limitation of the current work, which has its own focus on the tri-functions of this PF innovation. Therefore, we have added a limitation statement in the corresponding section. We hope our explanation is helpful. We still wish to thank the reviewer for this inquiry, which is about the core designing considerations within this work. This is actually one of our most important decisions made in preparing this paper, and we spend sufficient effort to ensure that the above-stated choice and details are based on theories and existing empirical work.

records.comment_text: 1. The Introduction currently provides an extensive overview of peer feedback in general. To enhance conciseness and focus, after briefly introducing the concept of peer feedback, the author should transition directly to discussing key concepts directly relevant to the study, such as dialogic peer feedback, GenAI-assisted peer feedback, and peer feedback self-efficacy.
records.response_text:
Response: Thanks for the comment. We tried to make the introduction section more concise. However, after several experiments with the introduction, we chose to keep its current main structure. From our perspective, the “main background -> gap -> purpose of the study” structure reads smooth and fit well with the theoretical and empirical background section towards framing the rationale and core research questions of the study.
Additionally, after experimenting, we felt hoisting the terminology or concept to an earlier position might not work as expected. This may be attributed to the fact that introducing the tri-functional perspective and constructing a model of GenAI-supported dialogic peer feedback are quite innovative, while many of the key terms might need them to be introduced in the first place for readers to fully grasp.
We still want to thank the reviewer for giving us this good opportunity to reflect upon the issue of conciseness. Although the size of revision we applied in this regard are not that substantial, but the readers would definitely benefit from the more concise presentation.
records.golden_move: We tried to make the introduction section more concise.

records.comment_text:
Thanks for being the editor of the manuscript SYS-D-25-01426R1 submitted to SYSTEM. After receiving the comments from the reviewers, we began to revise the paper.
We want to thank you and the reviewers for the review and comments. In this round of revision, we tried our best to tackle the issues suggested by the editor as well as reviewer #1. All the changes (apart from many minor changes in language use) in the manuscript are marked. We have also carefully responded to the reviewer’ comments which is presented in detail down below.
Thanks again for the editorial efforts and the support. Please address all correspondence to Dr. Da “Alex” Yan at alexyan1987@outlook.com. Thank you again for your consideration of this manuscript.
Regards,
The authors.
1. Please consider the point raised by Reviewer 1 regarding the addition of examples of peer-feedback to support the qualitative findings under 'Analysis'. It is great that you have added samples of both the experimental and control groups in Appendix D, but what is needed is more tangible examples in the body of the manuscript to help readers (including teachers) understand the type of feedback provided and how it leads to the conclusions.
records.response_text: Response: Thank you for enlightening us in addressing this issue. Frankly, the authors discussed and tried multiple approaches to address the lack of feedback examples in our previous revision effort. We only added an appendix because we didn’t find an effective way to incorporate the feedback messages into the results sections, which are dominated by statistical analyses. We attempted to integrate the feedback excerpts into the results sections as supportive evidence after the statistical analyses in this round of revision. Our specific answers to this revision request can be found in our responses to the comment by Reviewer #1 below. We thank the editor for clarifying the revision comment into actionable suggestions to follow.

records.comment_text: However, despite the authors' explanation, it is still necessary in my view to include 2-3 examples of the PF provided by the students to each other where relevant in the results section, perhaps for both experimental and control conditions. These examples should NOT be relegated to the appendix, but made front and centre in the results section, under the statistical analyses. This would help broaden the applicability of the paper to readers beyond statistical analysis, greatly enhancing its impact for teachers for example who can't follow/don't care about statistical analysis. I'm sure you are at the word limit but I'm also sure the editors won't mind if you go over a bit for this reason.
records.response_text:
Response: Thank you for the comment. During the first round of revision, we didn’t find an effective way to add feedback samples or excerpts directly into the body of the paper to provide evidence to complement the statistical analysis in the results sections. The comment from the reviewer (as well as the interpretation by the handling editor) helped us find a solution as requested. In this round, we added several short excerpts of student-generated feedback to support the results based on statistical analysis. We have also added a brief introduction to this method (in “Analysis” subsection) to maintain consistency between the methodology and the results.
However, we still kept what we have added in the appendix as is, since Appendix D serves as a valuable resource enabling readers to understand what a typical feedback comment from each group looks like, as well as how the feedback (after the re-feedback phase) is shaped through discussion and interactions. With Appendix D, we can confidently introduce the feedback excerpts in the results section without having to add underlying feedback dialogs each time (which would make the excerpted messages too long). Additionally, feedback messages in Appendix D can also be referred to in the results section as additional information.
Hopefully, the addition of the feedback excerpts will help make the paper more applicable to a broader range of readers.
records.golden_move: During the first round of revision, we didn’t find an effective way to add feedback samples or excerpts directly into the body of the paper to provide evidence to complement the statistical analysis in the results sections.
